lessons.title: Linked List Basics
lessons.concept: A linked list is nodes linked via pointers, allowing dynamic memory use. Singly linked: each node points to next. Access is O(n); insert/delete at known position O(1).
lessons.formula: Access: O(n); Insert/Delete at known node: O(1)
lessons.worked_example: Reverse singly linked list: use three pointers (prev, curr, next); reverse links iteratively.
mistakes: Forgetting to save next before reversing

lessons.title: Linked List vs Array
lessons.concept: Array: O(1) access, O(n) insert/delete (shift). Linked list: O(n) access, O(1) insert/delete at known node, no random access.
lessons.formula: Array access O(1); LL access O(n)
lessons.worked_example: Frequent insertions/deletions → linked list better. Frequent random access → array better.
mistakes: Choosing array for frequent middle insertions

practice.question: Better for frequent insertions and deletions?
practice.explanation: Linked lists support O(1) insertion/deletion at known positions; arrays require shifting O(n).

practice.question: A singly linked list node typically stores:

options.A: Data and a pointer/reference to the next node
options.B: Data and pointers to both neighbours only
options.D: A sorted key and a pivot

practice.explanation: Singly linked nodes hold data + next pointer; doubly linked nodes add a prev pointer as well.

practice.question: Head of a linked list points to:
practice.explanation: The head reference points at the first node; an empty list has head = null.

practice.question: The end of a singly linked list is marked by:

options.A: A sentinel pointing to the head

practice.explanation: The last node's next is null/None; that null terminates traversal.

practice.question: Which operation on a linked list is NOT O(1) even with a node reference?

options.A: Deleting the node after a given node
options.B: Finding the k-th node by index

practice.explanation: Locating the k-th node requires walking k links: O(k). Deletion/insertion around a known node and data updates are O(1).

practice.question: A doubly linked list adds which advantage over a singly linked list?

options.B: Backward traversal and O(1) deletion given the node (with its prev link)

practice.explanation: Each node keeps a prev pointer: traversal works in both directions and unlinking a known node updates prev/next directly. Random access still costs O(n).

questions.question: Data structure for to-do list where tasks added at end and processed in order added?
questions.explanation: Processed in order added → First-In-First-Out → Queue.

questions.question: Structure for managing function calls and local variables?
questions.explanation: Function call stack uses LIFO → stack.

questions.question: Structure for BFS in graph traversal?
questions.explanation: BFS uses a queue (FIFO) to explore level by level.

questions.question: Time to insert at end of singly linked list with tail pointer?
questions.explanation: With tail pointer, append directly → O(1).

questions.question: Average time to access the k-th element of a linked list (random k) is:
questions.explanation: No index arithmetic exists: the only way to reach node k is following next pointers k times -> O(k) average (O(n) worst case at the tail).

questions.question: What is the time complexity of inserting after a known node (given a reference to it)?
questions.explanation: Once the position is known, relinking two pointers (new.next = cur.next; cur.next = new) is constant time - unlike arrays, no shifting occurs.

questions.question: Deletion of a node in a singly linked list requires knowing:

options.B: The previous node (or copying data from the next node)

questions.explanation: To relink around a target you need its predecessor's next pointer; with only the target you can instead copy the next node's data and delete that successor.

questions.question: Main memory advantage of linked lists over arrays:

options.B: No preallocation - size grows/shrinks with nodes
options.C: They use more memory per element by design
options.D: They store pointers in the CPU cache

questions.explanation: Lists allocate per insert, so capacity tracks actual usage (though each node pays pointer overhead and locality is worse than arrays).

questions.question: Reversing a linked list iteratively runs in:

options.A: O(n) time and O(1) extra space
options.C: O(n) time but O(n) space always

questions.explanation: Three pointers (prev, cur, nxt) sweep the list once: O(n) time, O(1) space (recursion would use O(n) stack).
questions.provenance: Authored for BountyCode as original practice/question item; not scraped from third-party sources. Requires independent verification before TRUSTED promotion.

questions.question: Detecting a cycle in a linked list optimally uses:

options.A: A hash set of all nodes - required
options.B: Floyd's two-pointer (tortoise and hare) in O(1) space

questions.explanation: Slow and fast pointers meet if a cycle exists: O(n) time, O(1) space. A visited set also works but costs O(n) memory.

questions.question: Merging two SORTED linked lists of lengths m and n takes:
questions.explanation: The merge walk advances one pointer per step through both lists: O(m + n) time, O(1) auxiliary space (plus output links).
